vignette:
Ravi, a 34-year-old chaplain, had always found solace in his work, supporting those grappling with grief and loss. He believed that his role was a calling, a chance to bring comfort to others during their darkest moments. But after the traumatic event that occurred six months ago, he felt as though he was losing touch with that purpose. The mugging had been sudden and violent, robbing him not only of his belongings but of his sense of safety and control. As he walked home from a late-night service, he was ambushed by two men who emerged from the shadows, their faces obscured. The sharp glint of a knife and the menacing tone of their demands had sent waves of fear crashing over him. It was a night that had imprinted itself in his mind, turning into a series of fragmented images that replayed incessantly, leaving him feeling trapped in a loop of terror.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi found himself increasingly on edge. Crowded places had transformed from a mundane part of life to arenas of anxiety. Each time he stepped into a supermarket or attended a community gathering, he was engulfed by the sensation of being trapped, surrounded by too many people who could easily become threats. He could feel his heart racing, his breath quickening, and heavy breathing sounds from those around him would send him spiraling back to that dark night. Ravi had come to believe that such environments were dangerous, that he simply could not let his guard down. He started avoiding public spaces, opting to isolate himself at home, where he could control his surroundings, but the loneliness that ensued only deepened his sorrow.

Memories of the mugging haunted him relentlessly. At odd moments, when he was least expecting it, vivid images would flash before his eyes—a glint of steel, the men's angry voices, the smell of sweat and fear that had permeated the air that night. These sensory memories would flood him with rage, a rage that felt both empowering and terrifying. He would often find himself clenching his fists, wrestling with the anger that bubbled to the surface as he recalled the event. It was an anger directed not only at the assailants but also at himself. He believed deep down that the event had happened because of the sort of person he was; perhaps he had been too trusting or had failed to recognize the danger lurking in the dark. The thought gnawed at him, deepening his sense of helplessness. He felt as if he were constantly walking a tightrope, one slip away from disaster.

Ravi’s internal narrative spiraled further into self-criticism. He often compared himself to others, convinced that someone more vigilant or stronger wouldn’t have found themselves in such a vulnerable situation. This belief left him feeling isolated in his pain; he was certain that no one else would understand or would sympathize with his plight. The shame of being a victim compounded his loneliness, making it even more difficult to reach out for support. Instead, he poured himself into his work, but even there, he could feel a disconnect. It was as if he were performing a role rather than truly engaging with the people he was meant to help. His heart ached for connection, yet he felt as though he was standing on the periphery of his own life.

As time passed, the weight of his unprocessed trauma began to seep into his daily interactions. Friends and family expressed concern about his withdrawal, but Ravi brushed it off, convinced that he could navigate this alone. It wasn’t until a colleague at the chapel mentioned how lost he seemed that the reality of his situation began to sink in. The words pierced through his defenses, prompting a wave of shame and fear that he had been trying to ignore. He realized that the same darkness that had engulfed him after the mugging was now clouding his ability to be present in his work and relationships.

Finally, after days of sleepless nights and internal turmoil, Ravi found the courage to seek help. The thought of opening up about his trauma terrified him, yet he hoped that by sharing his story, he could begin to reclaim the life he had lost. He feared what lay ahead—would the pain ever truly fade? Could he find a way to feel safe again in the world he once embraced? But beneath that fear lay a flicker of hope, a belief that perhaps through this process, he could rediscover the joy and connection that had once defined his existence.
